turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Thursday, November 5th. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. And the Dow just had its best day in more than a year, because Washington changed hands and the oil price fell off a cliff on the same afternoon.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Start with the Iran file, because it is what moved the oil market. Reuters reports that mediators from Qatar and Pakistan are working on a narrower interim deal than anything on the table so far. The shape is a swap: Iran stops attacking shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and the United States ends its blockade of Iranian ports, with the nuclear questions pushed to a later round of talks.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The word to hold onto is "reportedly," because this is only partly corroborated so far. Tehran's public line is that Washington's latest reply was "not convincing," and the American side isn't speaking with one voice. Vice President Vance and envoy Witkoff are described as favoring a deal, while President Trump is keeping the option of more strikes open. The reason markets leaned into it anyway is that a narrow deal is the easiest kind to say yes to, since both sides can claim they gave up less than the other.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which connects to a second report that deserves a flag. The Atlantic, relayed by Israeli and American outlets, says the president has privately been questioning Defense Secretary Hegseth and Joint Chiefs chairman Caine over how the war has gone, and has asked advisers whether Hegseth should stay. CBS carries a version of the same account.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: These are accounts of private deliberations, not announced decisions, so treat them as a signal about the mood rather than a personnel story. The mood is that a president who just lost both chambers of Congress is deciding whether the next two years are about winning the war or ending it. You can see why Vance and Witkoff would use that window to push the deal, and why the market priced it in the same session.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Third, a small one with a big number behind it. Japan's health ministry data shows births to Japanese nationals rose in the first half of 2026, the first January-to-June increase in 11 years. The report is a headline-level item so far, so we'll hold the details, but the direction matters in a country where the birth count has fallen year after year.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: One half-year doesn't make a trend, and demographers will want to see whether it is a rebound from a depressed base or timing of marriages that were delayed. But for a country whose labor force and pension math both depend on that line, even a pause in the decline is worth a headline.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Chips took the after-hours hit. Qualcomm reported fiscal fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of $2.17 a share on $10.32 billion in revenue, which beat estimates. But the margin outlook and weakness in handset chips sent the stock down somewhere between 6% and 9% after the bell.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the pattern of this earnings season in miniature: a beat that doesn't matter, because the guide is what's priced. Handsets are the part of the Qualcomm business that depends on consumers, and the data-center and auto stories the bulls want to talk about are still too small to offset a soft phone cycle. Arm told the same story at a smaller scale. Royalty revenue rose 8% to $670 million, which was below forecasts, and the shares fell about 3% after hours.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And those two results were enough to rattle Asia, which we'll get to in a moment. Second story: Canva is restructuring, and the number is 1,271 employees, about 22% of the workforce. Not all of those are job losses, since some roles are being redeployed, but CEO Melanie Perkins called it "the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A design-software company that has been one of the great private tech success stories is cutting roughly a fifth of its staff, and the reason is the same one showing up across software: generative AI compresses the cost of making a design, which is the thing Canva sells. The restructuring is the company trying to move toward where the AI value is rather than defend where the old seats were.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And two calendar items to put on the board. Uber reports before the open this morning, with the consensus at 96 cents a share on $14.70 billion in revenue. And tomorrow is the October jobs report, which is the main event of the week.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The early estimates for payrolls are soft, around 40,000, with unemployment holding at 4.2%, after September came in at just 29,000. Treat the consensus as rough this early, but the shape is a labor market that has stopped adding jobs without yet shedding them, and that is exactly the kind of data that decides whether a Fed that just held keeps holding.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Europe had the cleaner day. The DAX rose 2.2% to 26,437, led by the banks, and the FTSE 100 gained 1.8% to 10,829. The read from European desks was that a Democratic Congress lowers the odds of an American trade escalation, and that cheaper oil is a gift to an energy-importing continent.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And the political reaction matched the market one. France's foreign minister called the Democratic wins "very good news for American democracy," and capitals across Europe are now doing the arithmetic on what a divided Washington means for tariffs, for Ukraine funding, and for how much of the Iran policy gets constrained by Congress. It's a soft quote, but it tells you where the allied sympathies sit.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Asia was the odd one out. Japan's Nikkei closed down 1.4% at 62,188, after being down more than 4% at one point in the session, on jitters about AI stocks and the Qualcomm and Arm read-through.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That intraday reversal is the thing I'd remember. A 4% drop that gets bought back to 1.4% says dip buyers are still active in Tokyo, but it also says the AI trade has become the single biggest swing factor for an index that used to trade on the yen and the Bank of Japan. When Nikkei sensitivity to a Qualcomm guide is that high, you are looking at a market that has become a levered expression of the chip cycle.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: This is the segment where we'd normally say the tape was quiet, and yesterday it wasn't. The Dow gained more than 1,500 points, about 3%, to close at 53,356, its best day since April of last year. The S&P 500 rose 1.6% to 7,688, and oil fell about 8%, with West Texas Intermediate settling around $88.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Two catalysts in one session, and it's worth separating them. The first is the election: with Democrats taking both chambers, investors read a lower probability of new tariffs and a higher probability of gridlock, and gridlock is historically something equities like. The second is oil, which is the one I'd watch, because it fell on de-escalation bets before there is any deal. If those mediators fail, a chunk of that move reverses.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Gold also jumped, about 3.3%, to around $4,070, which is an odd companion to a risk-on day.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It is odd until you realize that falling oil and rising gold are both a bet that the Fed has more room to ease. Lower energy prices cut the inflation risk, the Treasury 10-year fell about 6 basis points to roughly 4.89%, and metals responded to the lower real yield. The market is telling you it believes in disinflation from the supply side, not from weak demand, which is the better version of the story.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the cautionary note from the same session is what happened after the close. The Qualcomm and Arm moves, plus a neocloud selloff that was still deepening in Thursday futures, are the part of the market that isn't celebrating.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, so the picture is a broad rotation: energy stocks were the worst performers on the day, banks and cyclicals led, and the AI infrastructure complex is where the stress is. That's a market that is pricing a lower-oil, lower-rate, less-hyped world, and the full levels are on the Markets tab if you want them.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Today's deep dive is from The Economist, from the weekend package of pieces that ran around November 1st, under the headline "How the Houthis built their war machine." Full disclosure on sourcing: we have the newsletter framing and the headlines from the same package, and we've rebuilt the substance from open reporting, so we're not going to attribute to the article anything beyond what that framing supports.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The framing is vivid. The Economist's blurb says the Houthis "used to be dismissed as ragtag insurgents, or rebels in flipflops," and are now "one of the most dangerous militias in the Middle East." They've held northern Yemen for more than a decade, they've built a formidable arsenal of drones and missiles, and in recent weeks they've been striking Saudi Arabia, in the words of the piece, "one strike after another." Related headlines in the package say the group is "outgrowing its dependence on its patron," and that Saudi Arabia wants Iran to call off the Houthis and make a deal with America.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Let's put the thesis in plain terms. For a decade, the Houthis were the proxy that Iran armed and could point at when it wanted pressure on the Gulf. The argument now is that the proxy has turned into an industry: it can build or assemble a meaningful share of its own weapons, which means the relationship between patron and client is changing, and with it the logic of any deal Tehran might sign.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Start with what's solid. Iran's Quds Force has supplied components and technicians since around 2015, and a Seoul Economic Daily piece from late September describes Chinese commercial parts feeding the supply chain as well. The International Institute for Strategic Studies analyst Fabian Hinz is the useful skeptic here: he says the Houthis "remain dependent on Iran for key technologies and advanced capabilities." Those two points together are the real story. They can assemble simple ballistic missiles and drones in Yemen from commercial parts, but the advanced guidance and propulsion still come from outside.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Now the recent events. On October 13th, an administrative building at the Aramco site in Dhahran was targeted and a limited fire followed, though it's unclear whether it was a direct hit or interception debris, according to CNN. On October 25th, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted drones and missiles aimed at Riyadh, Khamis Mushait and the south, while the Houthis claimed targets at Yanbu that the coalition doesn't confirm.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And then the claims get thinner. Around October 30th the Houthis claimed six attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, at the same time that Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials were meeting Iranian officials in Tehran. One Saudi citizen was reportedly wounded by interception shrapnel over Riyadh. On November 3rd, the group claimed strikes on Abha airport, Khamis Mushait and Dammam. Much of this is self-reported, and we found no confirmed 2026 strike that actually damaged Aramco's production. That caveat matters, because the Houthis' media operation is part of the weapon.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So why does it matter to someone who works in energy? Because the economics are lopsided. A drone costs thousands or tens of thousands of dollars, and an interceptor missile costs orders of magnitude more. The defender spends a fortune to protect a facility, and the attacker only needs one leak.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly, and that cost curve is the second-order read. The Gulf is trying to build its AI and data-center ambitions on top of an energy infrastructure that is, for the first time since the 2019 Abqaiq attack, being probed with some regularity. That changes insurance pricing, it changes how you site critical load, and it changes how much of the region's buildout gets financed. Even when the strikes don't land, the cost of defending against them is a tax on every project.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The part I find most interesting is Riyadh's response. The reported Saudi position is to lean on Tehran rather than on Sanaa, which is an admission that the Saudis think the Houthis' leash still runs through Iran.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's also the point where the Economist's thesis is contested. If the Houthis are truly outgrowing their patron, then a US-Iran deal that includes the Hormuz swap we discussed wouldn't automatically stop the attacks on Saudi Arabia, because the group has its own production line and its own grievances. If they're still dependent on Iran for the advanced pieces, then a deal does constrain them, but only with a lag as stockpiles run down. Both readings are consistent with what we can see, and the honest answer is that we can't tell from the outside.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which means a deal in Doha might be necessary and not sufficient.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the cleanest way to say it. And one more caveat worth stating: this is the proxy-war version of the Iran story, not the headline version, and it's a front that the interim deal as described doesn't obviously address. If you're trying to forecast Gulf risk premiums, the Houthi line is the one that can embarrass a deal after it's signed.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Energy today starts with a piece from the SemiAnalysis newsletter that landed in the inbox on November 3rd, titled "Elon Is Doing It Again: SpaceX Will Be The World's Biggest AI Cloud." The paywall cuts off the economics, but the build-out numbers up front are the story.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: SemiAnalysis says SpaceX raised its 2027 data-center target from 10 gigawatts to roughly 13. It says 3.6 gigawatts is already under construction and it has identified more than 9 gigawatts of capacity in total. The comparison they draw is that this is roughly all of Google's data-center capacity from 1999 through 2026, built in about a year and a half.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the speed is the part practitioners will notice. Colossus 1 was a retrofit that took 122 days for 150 megawatts. Colossus 2 took 91 days for 210 megawatts. A hall they call Project SPAM started construction on October 5th with first tranches targeted for December, and a Mississippi site is on a roughly four-month schedule. The typical industry timeline they cite is 8 to 12 months.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So how do you power that? SemiAnalysis tracks more than 8 gigawatts of likely behind-the-meter capacity, against more than 9 gigawatts of data-center power coming online, which means power is being identified mid-build rather than secured first. Colossus 2's battery system is about 5.9 gigawatt-hours, possibly the largest in the US, and Starbase may use more than a gigawatt of aeroderivative turbines, with mobile units from Colossus 2 likely relocated there.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And here's the permit angle that makes this a practitioner's story. TVA says two projects, Macrohard at 700 megawatts and MiniHard at 450, have requested service, and a 500-kilovolt substation is due December 31st. The Southaven turbines can legally run at 2.7 gigawatts nameplate now, but only 1.24 gigawatts from July 2027 under a binding requirement signed on July 30th.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's a cliff. Per SemiAnalysis's math, the cliff leaves a gap of about 300 megawatts that batteries and a very low power usage effectiveness, around 1.10 to 1.15, have to cover. Their other claims are about labor, roughly 3,000 workers per gigawatt, and about a 10-gigawatt-plus chip fab concept in Grimes County, Texas, called TeraFab, which would likely get a data center for third-party renting. And their line is that deals with Anthropic and Google turned SpaceX into the most profitable neocloud.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Before you take the speed at face value, there's the counterweight. A report from Cleanview called "Bypassing the Grid" tracks 59 behind-the-meter data-center projects totalling about 90 gigawatts planned, with 92% of that announced just since 2025. Only about 2.2%, roughly 2 gigawatts, is operating, 1.2% is under construction, and 36% is permitted. About 60% is announcement or early stage.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's a sobering denominator. Cleanview's scenarios have cumulative behind-the-meter capacity as low as 5 gigawatts by the end of 2027, or about 13 gigawatts if every project with a signed tenant hits its timeline. Note that the report's figures have shifted between editions, so hold the exact numbers loosely, but the message is stable: the gap between announced and operating is enormous. SpaceX is the outlier that makes the optimistic case, not the median.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the tradeoff of going behind the meter is worth stating, since it's the through-line of the whole segment. You avoid the interconnection queue, but you take on fuel supply, emissions permitting, and reliability risk that a grid connection would have socialized.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, and permitting is where it bites, as the Southaven example shows. Speed buys you a first power date, but the air permit sets the ceiling on what you can run after it. The projects that look cheapest on day one can carry the most regulatory risk in year two.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Now the demand side. Meta's third quarter: revenue of $64.6 billion, up 26%, but capital spending of $34.9 billion against operating cash flow of $32.8 billion, so capex outran cash by about $2 billion for the quarter.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The full-year capex range was narrowed to $135 billion to $145 billion, with the low end raised from $130 billion. Nine-month spending is $85.8 billion, which by my arithmetic implies a fourth quarter somewhere between $49 billion and $59 billion. And there's no 2027 number. CFO Susan Li said the company is "still developing our budget and capacity plans for next year." The Hyperion campus in Louisiana has been reported as reset to 5 gigawatts and more than $50 billion, though one source calls the dollar figure unconfirmed, so treat that as a secondary-source claim.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And on the equipment side, GE Vernova's third quarter updates a story we've covered. Combined gas backlog and slot reservations rose from 116 gigawatts to 122, with a target of at least 130 by year end. The detail is the conversion: firm backlog went from 53 gigawatts to 64, while slot reservations fell from 63 to 58, which means about 13 gigawatts of reservations turned into orders.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That conversion is the thing to track. Reservations are options, orders are commitments, and a customer converting an option into a firm order is telling you the project is real. Power orders were $21.8 billion, up 178% organically, backlog is $197 billion, and gas turbines priced more than 20% above the fourth quarter of 2025. About 20% of GE Vernova's roughly 100 gas customers are data-center operators.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One for the calendar: Vistra reports third quarter results tomorrow at 10 a.m. Eastern, and its earlier anchors are a 20-year, 2,609-megawatt nuclear PPA with Meta from January, and a joint infrastructure vehicle with KKR and NVIDIA.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And Duke was scheduled to report today, with a preview citing a large-load pipeline in the mid-teens of gigawatts, but those preview numbers conflict across sources, so we'll wait for the actual release. The takeaway from the whole segment is that the equipment orders, the capex guides and the behind-the-meter build all point the same way, but the observed power actually delivered keeps lagging the announcements.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ngayong umaga, dalawang salita ang pag-aaralan natin, at pareho itong galing sa balita tungkol sa implasyon. Ang una ay "pagsipa."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang "pagsipa" ay galing sa salitang "sipa," at ang ibig sabihin nito sa balita ay biglaang pagtaas ng presyo o ng bilang. Mas matalim ang dating nito kaysa sa simpleng "pagtaas," dahil may kasamang gulat, parang may sumipa sa numero pataas.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Kaya sa mga ulat sa ekonomiya, makikita mo ang "pagsipa ng presyo ng gasolina" o "pagsipa ng implasyon." Kapag mabagal at paunti-unti ang pag-akyat, "pagtaas" ang gamit. Kapag biglaan at nakagugulat, "pagsipa."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tama. At hindi ito masyadong pormal, pero tanggap na tanggap sa balita at sa diyaryo. Hindi ito balbal, kaya ligtas gamitin sa isang usapang seryoso.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang ikalawang salita ay "tumindi," galing sa "tindi," na ibig sabihin ay tindi o bigat ng isang bagay.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ginagamit ang "tumindi" kapag lumalala ang isang sitwasyon o damdamin. Tumindi ang init, tumindi ang galit, tumindi ang hirap ng mga tsuper. May ideya ito ng pag-igting na unti-unting dumarating.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Magkaiba ito sa "lumala," na mas pangkalahatan. Ang "lumala" ay basta sumama ang kalagayan. Ang "tumindi" ay may dagdag na bigat, na parang pasanin na lalong bumibigat.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Subukan natin sa pangungusap. Dahil sa pagsipa ng presyo ng pamasahe, tumindi ang hirap ng mga komyuter noong Oktubre.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Magaling. Pakinggan ninyo ang dalawang salitang iyan sa balitang Pilipinas na susunod.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Pumalo sa 7.8% ang implasyon sa Pilipinas noong Oktubre, mas mataas kaysa 7.2% noong Setyembre. Ito ang pinakamataas ngayong 2026, at pinakamabilis mula pa noong Pebrero 2023.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Dahil sa pagsipa ng presyo ng pamasahe at gasolina, tumindi ang pasanin ng mga ordinaryong pamilya. Umabot sa 20.1% ang implasyon sa transportasyon, at ramdam ito ng bawat komyuter sa jeepney at bus.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Tumama ang bilang sa mataas na dulo ng inaasahan ng mga ekonomista, at pasok pa rin sa hanay na 7.1% hanggang 8.1% na itinakda ng Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Now in English for the detail. The print beat the BusinessWorld poll median of 7.6% and the Manila Times poll of 7.7%, though it stayed inside the central bank's own forecast range. The average for January through October is 5.6%, so the year is running far below the monthly peak, but the monthly line has now broken higher.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The geography is revealing. In Metro Manila, inflation was 5.9%, up from 5.3%. Outside the capital it was 8.2%, up from 7.6%. So the provinces, where commuting by jeepney and tricycle and buying rice and fuel take a bigger share of the budget, are feeling it more than the capital.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And that is the headline-versus-household story. Transport at 20.1% is a weighted component, and it's the one the central bank can do least about, since fares and gasoline respond to oil and the peso. What we didn't retrieve this morning is core inflation or the central bank's reaction, and sources differ on whether the target is a flat 3% or a 2% to 4% range, so we'll wait for the BSP's statement before drawing a conclusion on policy.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The peso is part of the story. It was around 63.5 to the dollar on Wednesday, off the record low of 64.17 reached last week, with the weakness being the transmission mechanism: a weaker peso makes imported fuel more expensive in pesos, which feeds directly into that transport number.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And the oil drop on Wednesday is, in principle, the best news these households could get. If the de-escalation bets hold, the fuel component should ease in the coming months. But pump prices lag crude, and a record-low peso offsets some of it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: On the budget, the Senate returns to plenary on November 9th, with the aim of having the budget signed by the second week of December. One number to note: the National Expenditure Program carried 11,420 DPWH projects, versus 16,244 in the House version, which is the size of the gap the Senate is reviewing.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Senator Lacson says the review will extend to projects in the district of Sandro Marcos, the president's son, and the Palace says it won't allow undocumented amendments. We covered the purge and the veto earlier this week, so the new information is the date and the project counts, and the date is the one that matters: the Senate has about a month to reconcile two very different lists.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The through-line connecting both stories is who absorbs the cost, and in the Philippines this morning the answer is households, through fares, and taxpayers, through a budget that is still being cleaned up.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two Mandarin words today, and both come from the China story that follows. The first is 即便, meaning "even if" or "even though," and it is the formal cousin of the everyday 就算.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a concessive connective: you grant a hypothetical and then say the conclusion holds anyway. It usually pairs with 也 or 还 in the second half. For example: 即便融资成本下降,企业也不一定愿意扩大投资。(Even if financing costs fall, companies aren't necessarily willing to expand investment.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In register, 即便 sits on the written side, so you'll see it in news and analysis, whereas in conversation people would say 就算. It's also stronger than 如果, which is just "if," because 即便 admits that the condition is real and says the conclusion survives it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The second word is 抑制, meaning to curb or suppress. It's formal, and it collocates with abstract nouns such as demand, inflation, growth and sentiment. For example: 价格下降抑制了企业的利润。(Falling prices curbed corporate profits.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The near-synonym is 控制, which just means "to control," and is neutral. 抑制 carries the sense of pressing something down, so you'd say 抑制通胀 for curbing inflation, and 抑制需求 for suppressing demand. Listen for both in the China segment.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 即便央行降低了融资成本,投资者仍然很谨慎。(Even if the central bank has lowered financing costs, investors are still very cautious.)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Let's make that concrete. China's stock market rebounded sharply, with the Shanghai Composite up 2.16% to about 3,686. The People's Bank of China cut the rate on its relending facility for stock buybacks and shareholding increases to 1.00% from 1.25%, though the date of that cut is unverified in the sources we found. A one-year securities swap facility for brokers, funds and insurers also launched on November 3rd, and 31 firms applied for more than 100 billion yuan.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 价格下降抑制了企业的利润,这也是服务业数据传递的信号。(Falling prices curbed corporate profits, and that is also the signal from the services data.)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The services PMI from RatingDog, formerly Caixin, was 50.8 in October, down from 51.6 in September, the weakest since July but still expanding. The detail is the pairing: companies are cutting prices while their own costs are rising. New export business in services rose for a sixth straight month, which is the bright spot.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the goods side is softer. The official export orders sub-index fell to 48.7 from 50.0, and a private survey shows export prices falling for the first time since November of last year.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So here's the debt-deflation lens. The authorities are using cheap, targeted liquidity to put a floor under equities, because a stock market that rises helps balance sheets and confidence, but the real economy is showing margin pressure from falling prices. 即便 the equity channel works, it doesn't fix what the PMI says about pricing power.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Worth watching: October customs trade data is due within a day or two, and one forecast has the 2026 surplus possibly topping last year's record of $1.2 trillion, though we couldn't verify that figure. If export prices are falling while volumes hold, the surplus is a measure of China exporting its deflation, and that is the trade-politics story for the next year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Literature first. China Miéville won the Goldsmiths Prize on Wednesday for The Rouse, published by Picador, which carries £10,000 and is awarded for fiction that breaks the mold. It's the longest novel ever to win since the prize began in 2013, at roughly 1,250 pages, and reports say he spent about 20 years on it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The judges were chaired by Francis Spufford, with Kate Briggs, Hari Kunzru and David Sexton. Paraphrasing the judges' comments, the shortlist was uniformly strong, but this was the book that broke most sharply with expectations, in ambition, in its use of history and in linguistic experiment. Kunzru called it a monumental work. The book moves through decades of British imperial and Cold War history, which is an unusual canvas for a writer best known for weird fiction.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The shortlist around it is a good reading list: Polly Barton's What Am I, A Deer? from Fitzcarraldo, Doireann Ní Ghríofa's Said the Dead from Faber, and Keith Ridgway's Dooneen, also Fitzcarraldo. The prize's own shortlist headline was "Newness of many different kinds."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And the bigger prize is on Monday. The Booker winner will be announced on November 9th at Old Billingsgate in London, with £50,000 for the winner. The six on the shortlist are M. John Harrison's The End of Everything, Marlon James's The Disappearers, Luke Kennard's Black Bag, Douglas Stuart's John of John, Elizabeth Strout's The Things We Never Say, and Rebecca Perry's May We Feed the King.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two of those authors have won before: Marlon James and Douglas Stuart. Harrison is 81, so he would be the oldest winner in the prize's history, and Strout is on her second shortlisting.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Second item, in visual art, and it's a detective story. A 17th-century Dutch painting by Willem Cornelisz Duyster, "Un Buveur," or "The Drinker," is returning to Orléans after 86 years. It was looted from the city's museum in June 1940, when the museum was ransacked and set on fire.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A former Orléans antiques dealer, Jean-Bernard Rouilly, spotted it in the catalogue of an October 17th auction at Gloggner in Lucerne. It was first thought to be a study, then confirmed as the original. The current owner had bought it at a London auction in the 1990s and, on learning the provenance, immediately proposed to return it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's reportedly held at customs now, with a return expected within weeks. It's also the first result of the museum's "Wanted" poster campaign: four paintings have been returned in total, and somewhere around 424 to 427 are still missing, depending on the source. What I like about it is that the return came from a catalogue, which says the missing-art problem is partly a distribution-of-attention problem.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two takes on the midterms, pulling in opposite directions. First, Robby Soave in The Hill, under the headline "Republicans annihilated in midterms: Anti-war MAGA was right." We read the snippet and listing rather than the full column, so we'll stick to what it says.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: His argument is that Republicans lost the House and the Senate by more than even partisan observers expected, and that the hawks who predicted a quick end to the Iran war, or said it wouldn't affect the midterms, were wrong. The frame is that the restraint wing of the movement was vindicated. He also notes that Trump pledged to accept the results, work with Democrats where possible and veto bad legislation.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The steelman is real: if you believe voters punished a war they were told would be short, then the restrainers called it. The counter-take is that the causes were mixed. The Wall Street Journal's framing was that Democrats coalesced around the economy to pull off the win, and Mitt Romney, in the Deseret News, blamed "bad policy, bad character." Neither of those is an anti-war explanation.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And one of Soave's own premises is in tension with a same-day headline, CBS reporting the president saying he has "ultimate power" to block Democrats. A man pledging to work with the other side and claiming ultimate power to stop it in the same news cycle is a position you have to test, not assume. The restraint-wing story is plausible, but it's an interpretation, and exit polls will tell us more than columnists will.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The second piece pulls the other way. Jennifer Graham, in the Deseret News, wrote "The good news for all Americans in the midterm shellacking." Her argument is that the results, which hand both chambers to Democrats and thwart the Republican agenda, should "silence the incessant doom chatter about American democracy being at risk because of Donald J. Trump."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The steelman there is institutional. Elections were held, power is changing hands, the checks are working, and a system that does that is resilient. It's a fair corrective to a year of predictions that the midterms might not happen or wouldn't be respected.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The counter is the same CBS headline. Resilience is not demonstrated by one election night but by what happens in the next two years when a president with an expanded view of executive power meets a Congress that wants to constrain him. The test isn't the vote; it's the subpoena, the budget and the veto.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Put the two columns side by side and the disagreement is instructive. Soave reads the result as a verdict on a policy, the war. Graham reads it as a verdict on a system, the democracy. Both can be true, but they imply opposite things about what the winners should do next.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One Good Thing. Trevor Bergman is 59 and a police officer in Melbourne, and he has donated blood and plasma 545 times, and he has done it at every one of the 85 Lifeblood donation centres in Australia.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: He's one of about 150 Australians who carry a rare anti-D antibody, which makes his plasma the raw material for anti-D immunoglobulin, the treatment given to pregnant mothers when their newborns are at risk of hemolytic disease. He started giving at 18, and the idea of visiting every centre came about a decade ago on a holiday in Perth.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The final stop was Canberra in May, and the Governor-General, Sam Mostyn, donated alongside him. His most memorable moment on the tour was the one time he was turned away, for being unwell, in Albany, Western Australia.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And the timing is a good reminder. Lifeblood put out an urgent call this month after blood and plasma supplies hit a ten-year low, and donations have picked up since. Bergman isn't a record-holder, since James Harrison gave more than 1,100 times, but the point isn't the number. It's a man who found out he carried something rare and decided to spend his weekends turning it into protection for strangers' babies.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's The Morning Commute for Thursday, November 5th. Thanks for listening.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Have a good day, and we'll see you tomorrow, with the jobs report.
